title: AEMO's Integrated System Plan relies on gas-fired generation to firm renewables through the 2030s and beyond
oneLiner: The market operator's own plan keeps gas peakers in the mix as backup, run for a small number of hours a year.
body: In every Integrated System Plan scenario, gas-fired peaking plants remain in the system to cover long periods of low wind and solar output. Their capacity is held or grows while their total energy output falls, because they run rarely.
contextBackground: This is one of the few points on which the market operator, gas producers and most renewable advocates agree in substance while disagreeing in emphasis: gas as insurance, running rarely, is part of the plan.
contextDisagreement: The dispute is over quantity and duration: how many hours a year, for how many decades, and whether storage or hydrogen displaces it sooner than the plan assumes.

evidenceItems.citation: Australian Energy Market Operator, Integrated System Plan — role of gas-powered generation

otherClaim.title: Nuclear power cannot help with Australia's electricity prices or reliability in time to matter

claimItself.title: Nuclear power cannot help with Australia's electricity prices or reliability in time to matter
claimItself.oneLiner: The pressure on bills and on the grid is this decade; a first reactor is the decade after next.
claimItself.body: The case for repeal is usually made in terms of today's problems: high bills, coal plants closing, a grid under strain. Each of those plays out in the 2020s and 2030s. Even on generous assumptions nothing nuclear would generate before 2040, by which time the coal fleet has closed and the firming it needed has been built from something else.

ownArguments.label: FOR
ownArguments.text: A first Australian nuclear power reactor could not be generating electricity before 2040

ownArguments.label: FOR

otherClaim.title: The east-coast gas reservation scheme starting in July 2027 will materially lower domestic gas prices

claimItself.title: The east-coast gas reservation scheme starting in July 2027 will materially lower domestic gas prices
claimItself.oneLiner: Australia has decided to reserve gas for domestic buyers. The question now is whether the scheme, as designed and then softened, will do what it was announced to do.
claimItself.body: In May 2026 the federal government announced that Queensland's three LNG export ventures must reserve a share of export volumes for Australian users from July 2027, with contracts signed before 22 December 2025 exempt. In September 2026 the rule was recast around forecast domestic demand rather than a flat share of exports. The government says prices will fall; it will not say by how much.

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: Because export contracts signed before 22 December 2025 are exempt, the scheme reaches too little gas to move prices for years

ownArguments.label: FOR
ownArguments.text: Western Australia requires LNG projects to reserve 15 per cent of production for the domestic market, and its gas prices have been well below the east coast's

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: Mandatory reservation will deter investment in new gas supply and worsen the shortfall it is meant to fix

otherClaim.title: Keeping gas supply projects in the slowest approval lane conflicts with the government's reliance on new gas for firming and for the reservation scheme

claimItself.title: Keeping gas supply projects in the slowest approval lane conflicts with the government's reliance on new gas for firming and for the reservation scheme
claimItself.oneLiner: The industry's objection to the exclusion, and the point where the energy and environment debates meet.
claimItself.body: The market operator's plan keeps gas-fired generation as firming through the 2030s, and the east-coast reservation scheme depends on new supply coming on. Excluding gas projects from streamlined assessment means the supply the government is counting on faces the longest process in the system.
